---
title: "Packages for Epi Work"
---

R has thousands of packages. That number is genuinely overwhelming when
you're starting out, and you don't need most of it. Real epidemiology
work — loading data, cleaning it, summarizing it, mapping it, sharing it
— runs on a small, learnable core. This page is that core: a
"which package for which job" map, grouped by task, with a pointer to
the chapter where the book actually teaches each one.

It's deliberately short and opinionated. It is **not** a tour of CRAN.
If a package isn't here, it's usually because you don't need it yet —
not because it doesn't exist.

::: {.callout-note}
## The tidyverse umbrella
Many of these packages ship together under the
[tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/). One `library(tidyverse)` call
loads `readr`, `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `stringr`, `lubridate`, `ggplot2`, and
more all at once. The book loads them **individually** so it's always
obvious which package a function comes from — but once you know your way
around, the umbrella call is a fine shortcut.
:::

## Data ingestion — getting data in and out

Reading raw files into R and writing results back out.

| Package | What it's for | Where it's taught |
|---|---|---|
| `readr` | Read and write CSVs and other delimited text files | [Loading Your First Dataset](../01-working-with-real-data/index.qmd) |
| `here` | Build project-relative file paths that just work | [Loading Your First Dataset](../01-working-with-real-data/index.qmd) |
| `readxl` | Read data out of Excel workbooks (`.xlsx`) | [Working with Excel Files](excel-files.qmd) |
| `writexl` | Write data to Excel workbooks for colleagues who live in Excel | [Working with Excel Files](excel-files.qmd) |
| `fs` | Work with files and folders — create, copy, list directory trees | [Writing Data Files](writing-files.qmd) |

## Data manipulation and management — reshaping and cleaning

The everyday workhorses. Most of your time is spent here.

| Package | What it's for | Where it's taught |
|---|---|---|
| `dplyr` | Filter, select, mutate, group, and summarize rows and columns | [Loading Your First Dataset](../01-working-with-real-data/index.qmd) |
| `tidyr` | Reshape between long and wide; pivot, separate, and tidy up | [Cleaning Data](../02-cleaning-data/index.qmd) |
| `janitor` | Clean messy column names and make quick cross-tabs | [Cleaning Data](../02-cleaning-data/index.qmd) |
| `lubridate` | Parse and do math with dates and times | [Cleaning Data](../02-cleaning-data/index.qmd) |
| `stringr` | Find, match, and reshape text and character data | [Cleaning Data](../02-cleaning-data/index.qmd) |
| `glue` | Build strings by dropping variables straight into text | [Cleaning Data](../02-cleaning-data/index.qmd) |

## Data analysis — describing your data

Here's the honest picture: the book currently does its descriptive work
— counts, rates, group summaries — with `dplyr::summarise()` and
friends. That covers a surprising amount of real reporting.

Dedicated statistics packages (for regression, cross-tabulations,
age-adjusted rates, survival, and the like) are a **future addition** to
this book rather than something it teaches today. When they arrive,
they'll show up here. For now, `dplyr` is your analysis engine.

## Data visualization — charts, maps, and tables

| Package | What it's for | Where it's taught |
|---|---|---|
| `ggplot2` | Build charts layer by layer — the standard for R graphics | [Visualizing Your Data](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd) |
| `sf` | Hold and manipulate spatial (geographic) data as tidy tables | [Visualizing Your Data](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd) |
| `tigris` | Download US Census geographies (town, county, tract boundaries) | [Visualizing Your Data](../03-data-visualization/index.qmd) |
| `leaflet` | Build interactive, zoomable web maps | [Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet](../03-data-visualization/mapview-leaflet.qmd) |
| `mapview` | Get a quick interactive look at spatial data in one line | [Interactive Maps: mapview & leaflet](../03-data-visualization/mapview-leaflet.qmd) |
| `gt` | Build polished, publication-ready tables | Not yet covered — the go-to when the book adds table formatting |

## Reproducible practices and getting data

Pulling data from the web, and turning your analysis into something you
can hand off.

| Package / Tool | What it's for | Where it's taught |
|---|---|---|
| `httr2` | Talk to web APIs to pull data directly into R | [Working with APIs and Functions](../apis-functions/index.qmd) |
| Quarto | Turn code, prose, and results into reproducible reports, sites, and documents | This entire book is built with it — see [quarto.org](https://quarto.org/) |

## A note on this list

This is a small core, chosen so you can actually learn it — not a
complete inventory. It will grow as the book grows (dedicated stats and
table-formatting packages are on the way). When a task isn't listed
here, that's usually a sign the book hasn't taught it yet, and inventing
a package for it would only add to the overwhelm this page is trying to
cut.
